extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, physicists, and advanced students/scholars of classical mechanics (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: A sequence of propositions, lemmas, problems and corollaries from Newton's Principia treating laws of centripetal/attractive forces for spherical and non‑spherical bodies, and methods for computing resultant attractions and motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXV. Theor. XXXV
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad Sphæræ datæ puncta singula tendant vires æquales centripetæ decrescentes in duplicata ratione distantiarum a punctis, dico quod Sphæra quævis alia similaris attrahitur vi reciproce proportionali quadrato distantiæ centrorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: reduces the attraction of a whole sphere to that of a single central particle using previous theorems (notably Theorems XXXI and XXXIV). Corollaries: (1) Attraction of homogeneous spheres to other spheres is proportional to their contents applied to the squares of distances between centers; (2) same when the attracted sphere also attracts (mutual attraction doubles by Newton's 3rd law proportion preserved); (3–4) analogous statements hold for motion about umbilics (conic sections) whether bodies move inside or outside the attracting sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXVI. Theor. XXXVI
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Sphæræ in progressu a centro ad circumferentiam (quod materiæ densitatem & vim attractivam) utcunq; dissimilares, in progressu vero per circuitum ad datam omnem a centro distantiam sunt undiq; similares, & vis attractiva puncti cujusq; decrescit in duplicata ratione distantiæ corporis attracti: dico quod vis tota qua hujusmodi Sphæra una attrahit aliam sit reciproce proportionalis quadrato distantiæ centrorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive proof: represent any sphere as sum/difference of concentric similar shells; apply Prop. LXXV to each shell and integrate in the infinitesimal limit; obtain inverse-square dependence of total attraction between spheres regardless of internal radial density profile. Corollaries (1–9): mutual attraction proportionalities for multiple similar spheres, relations for motional periods when spheres rotate, and extensions to spheres located at umbilics or gyrating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXVII. Theor. XXXVII
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad singula Sphærarum puncta tendant vires centripetæ proportionales distantiis punctorum a corporibus attractis: dico quod vis composita, qua Sphæræ duæ se mutuo trahent, est ut distantia inter centra Sphærarum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several cases (Cas. 1–6) show by integrating planar and spherical contributions that when pointwise centripetal forces are proportional to the distance to the attracted body, the total attraction between two spheres is proportional to the distance between their centers (i.e., linear dependence). Includes argument reducing a sphere to a central equivalent particle. Mutual attraction doubles when both exert forces. Cases cover interior and exterior placements of the attracted particle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXVIII. Theor. XXXVIII
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Sphæræ in progressu a centro ad circumferentiam sint utcunq; dissimilares & inæquabiles, in progressu vero per circuitum ad datam omnem a centro distantiam sint undiq; similares; & vis attractiva puncti cujusq; sit ut distantia corporis attracti: dico quod vis tota qua hujusmodi Sphæræ duæ se mutuo trahunt sit proportionalis distantiæ inter centra Sphærarum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated from the preceding proposition in the same manner as Prop. LXXVII was deduced from LXXV. Corollary: prior results about motion in conic sections apply when attractions obey the stated law and bodies are of the described condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium on attraction cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion: two most notable cases of attractions were given—(i) centripetal forces decreasing in the duplicate ratio of distances (inverse-square), and (ii) centripetal forces increasing in the simple ratio of distances—both produce motion in conic sections and the corresponding laws for spherical components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton notes other cases produce less elegant conclusions; he prefers a general method to encompass and determine all such cases. This scholium frames the general approach used in subsequent propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXIX
rubrics_metrics.description: If circles with centres S and P produce arcs EF and ef whose distance tends to zero, then the ultimate ratio of the vanishing line Dd to the vanishing line Ff is the same as that of PE to PS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric lemma about limiting ratios of infinitesimal elements on concentric constructions. Proof uses similar triangles and limiting arguments; used to relate surface/line element ratios in later integration-style arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXIX. Theor. XXXIX
rubrics_metrics.description: Si superficies ob latitudinem infinite diminutam jamjam evanescens EFfe, convolutione sui circa axem PS, describat solidum Sphæricum concavo-convexum, ad cujus particulas singulas æquales tendant æquales vires centripetæ: dico quod vis, qua solidum illud trahit corpusculum situm in P, est in ratione composita ex ratione solidi DEq. × Ff & ratione vis qua particula data in loco Ff traheret idem corpusculum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how the attraction of a thin spherical shell (generated by revolving an infinitesimal arc) on a particle at P factors into geometric factors: DE^2 × Ff times the local particle force. Proof uses decomposition into infinitesimal elements and Archimedean results relating surface annuli to line elements. This result is a building block for integrating full spherical surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXX. Theor. XL
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad Sphæræ alicujus AEB, centro S descriptæ, particulas singulas æquales tendant æquales vires centripetæ, & ad Sphæræ axem AB, in quo corpusculum aliquod P locatur, erigantur de punctis singulis D perpendicula DE, Sphæræ occurrentia in E, & in ipsis capiantur longitudines DN, quæ sint ut quantitas DEq. × PS ÷ PE & vis quam Sphæræ particula sita in axe ad distantiam PE exercet in corpusculum P conjunctim: dico quod vis tota, qua corpusculum P trahitur versus Sphæram, est ut area comprehensa sub axe Sphæræ AB & linea curva ANB, quam punctum N perpetuo tangit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduces attraction of whole spherical surface to an area under a curve ANB traced by ordinates DN; uses the previous lemma and Proposition LXXIX. Corollaries give special cases when particle forces follow particular power laws (e.g., constant, inverse, inverse-square, inverse-cube) and show how DN is chosen accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXI. Prob. XLI (measure area ABNA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the preceding constructions, the problem is to measure the area ABNA (the area whose ordinate construction gives the total attraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive method: tangent from P, normal, bisection etc. Expansion of DE^2/(PE×V) into three parts yields three corresponding curve contributions whose areas are known by standard methods; three worked examples for particular force laws are given: (1) centripetal force ∝ 1/distance, (2) ∝ 1/distance^3, (3) ∝ 1/distance^4, each leading to explicit area constructions (e.g., hyperbolic sections) and giving the total attraction (example 3 yields attraction ∝ SI^3/PI). The proposition demonstrates how to convert infinitesimal element formulas into classical geometrical quadratures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXII. Theor. XLI
rubrics_metrics.description: In Sphæra centro S intervallo SA descripta, si capiantur SI, SA, SP continue proportionales: dico quod corpusculi intra Sphæram in loco quovis I attractio est ad attractionem ipsius extra Sphæram in loco P, in ratione composita ex dimidiata ratione distantiarum a centro IS, PS & dimidiata ratione virium centripetarum, in locis illis P & I, ad centrum tendentium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States the relationship between attraction inside and outside a sphere when SI, SA, SP are in continued proportion: attraction at an interior point I relates to that at exterior P by composed half-ratios of distances and half-ratios of local centripetal force magnitudes. Proof uses the ordinate DN formula from previous proposition and algebraic substitution for power-law force dependencies; special cases illustrate inverse-square, inverse-cube, inverse-fourth laws where interior/exterior ratios simplify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXIII. Prob. XLII
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire vim qua corpusculi in centro Sphæræ locatum ad ejus segmentum quodcunq; attrahitur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: find the force with which a given spherical segment attracts a particle at the sphere's center. Uses a physical (finite thickness) spherical surface to get PF×DF×O proportionality and assumes pointwise forces ∝ 1/D^{n} to derive that the total force of the segment is represented by an ordinate construction FN whose applied area describes the attracting force (provides method for converting surface segments into effective ordinates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXIV. Prob. XLIII
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire vim qua corpusculum, extra centrum Sphæræ in axe segmenti cujusvis locatum, attrahitur ab eodem segmento.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a segment EBK attracting a body P located on its axis, the attraction of the first part is found by Prop. LXXXI and of the second by LXXXIII; sum yields the whole segment's attraction. The proposition prescribes decomposition into parts and recomposition to compute forces for off-center axial points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium: transition to non-spherical bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: After treating spherical bodies, Newton remarks he could proceed to laws of attraction for other bodies composed of attractible particles but prefers to add more general propositions for use in philosophy rather than treat each case particle-by-particle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames the transition to Section XIII, indicating that general propositions will be given instead of exhaustive particle-level treatments for every shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXV. Theor. XLII
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corporis attracti, ubi attrahenti contiguum est, attractio longe fortior sit, quam cum vel minimo intervallo separantur ab invicem: vires particularum trahentis, in recessu corporis attracti, decrescunt in ratione plusquam duplicata distantiarum a particulis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If attraction in contact is much stronger than at finite separation, then the particle forces of the attracting body must decrease, as the attracted body recedes, in a ratio more than inverse-square. Argument uses comparison with spherical case (Prop. LXXIV) and notes that for concave/convex spherical shells, internal cancellation can make contact produce little change unless the local law is sufficiently steep. Concludes general proposition for bodies of arbitrary shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXVI. Theor. XLIII
rubrics_metrics.description: Si particularum, ex quibus corpus attractivum componitur, vires in recessu corporis attracti decrescunt in triplicata vel plusquam triplicata ratione distantiarum a particulis: attractio longe fortior erit in contactu, quam cum attrahens & attractum intervallo vel minimo separantur ab invicem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If pointwise forces decay as inverse-cube or faster, attraction upon contact becomes arbitrarily large (diverges) compared to finite separation—demonstrated by examples from Problem XLI showing infinite growth of attraction in approach. Extends to spherical and concavo-convex bodies by comparison and by adding/subtracting shells anywhere away from the contact point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXVII. Theor. XLIV
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpora duo sibi invicem similia & ex materia æqualiter attractiva constantia seorsim attrahant corpuscula sibi ipsis proportionalia & ad se similiter posita: attractiones acceleratrices corpusculorum in corpora tota erunt ut attractiones acceleratrices corpusculorum in eorum particulas totis proportionales & in totis similiter positas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two bodies made of equal-attractivity matter consist of particles proportional to the whole and similarly situated, then the net accelerative attractions of particles in the whole bodies scale as the attractions between corresponding particles; by partition and recomposition, the attraction between whole bodies follows from attractions between corresponding elements. Corollaries: deduce how total attractions scale with body sizes when pointwise forces follow various power laws (inverse-square, inverse-cube, inverse-fourth), yielding proportionalities in terms of linear dimensions, volumes, or reciprocals as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXVIII. Theor. XLV
rubrics_metrics.description: Si particularum æqualium corporis cujuscunq; vires attractivæ sint ut distantiæ locorum a particulis: vis corporis totius tendet ad ipsius centrum gravitatis; & eadem erit cum vi globi ex materia consimili & æquali constantis & centrum habentis in ejus centro gravitatis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a body's equal particles exert attractive forces proportional to their distances to the attracted point, then the resultant force of the whole body tends to (and equals) that as if all mass were concentrated at the body's center of gravity; by pairwise decomposition the lateral components cancel leaving a central resultant. Corollary: motion of attracted body will be as if attracted by a spherical body located at its center of gravity (elliptical orbits if center moves uniformly or is fixed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXIX. Theor. XLVI
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Corpora sint plura ex particulis æqualibus constantia, quarum vires sunt ut distantiæ locorum a singulis: vis ex omnium viribus composita, qua corpusculum quodcunq; trahitur, tendet ad trahentium commune centrum gravitatis, & eadem erit ac si trahentia illa, servato communi gravitatis centro, coirent & in globum formarentur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extends Prop. LXXXVIII to multiple bodies: for several bodies made of equal particles whose pointwise forces ∝ distance, the composite attraction tends to the common center of gravity and equals that of the bodies concentrated at that center. Corollary: motion of attracted body is as if the attracting bodies coalesced into a single spherical mass at their common center of gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XC. Prob. XLIV
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad singula circuli cujuscunq; puncta tendant vires centripetæ decrescentes in quacunq; distantiarum ratione: invenire vim qua corpusculum attrahitur ubivis in recta quæ ad planum circuli per centrum ejus perpendicularis consistit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a method to find the attraction on a point P located on the axis perpendicular to the plane of a circle: reduce the annuli contributions to an area AHILK whose area times AP gives the attraction. Corollaries: specializations for inverse-square and general inverse-power laws; if the circle's diameter tends to infinity, one obtains the attraction of an infinite plane (force ∝ 1/PA^{n-2}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XCI. Prob. XLV
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire attractionem corpusculi siti in axe solidi, ad cujus puncta singula tendunt vires centripetæ in quacunq; distantiarum ratione decrescentes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a solid with axis AB, cut by planes perpendicular to axis to obtain circular sections; use Prop. XC to get the ordinate FK for each cross-section, and the total attraction equals the area LABI traced by the curve LKI. Corollaries: (1) for a cylinder with inverse-square pointwise forces, attraction on axis P equals AB - PE + PD; (2) gives formulae for spheroids and their axial attractions by reducing to comparable spherical cases and computing section areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XCII. Prob. XLVI
rubrics_metrics.description: Dato corpore attractivo, invenire rationem decrementi virium centripetarum in ejus puncta singula tendentium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given an attracting body, one can find a regular shape (sphere, cylinder, etc.) whose attraction law matches the body's decrement law (using Propositions LXXX–LXXXI & XCI). By experiment measuring attraction at different distances, one can deduce the pointwise law (exponent n) of decrement of the forces of constituent particles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XCIII. Theor. XLVII
rubrics_metrics.description: Si solidum ex una parte planum, ex reliquis autem partibus infinitum, constet ex particulis æqualibus æqualiter attractivis, quarum vires in recessu a solido decrescunt in ratione potestatis cujusvis distantiarum plusquam quadraticæ, & vi solidi totius corpusculum ad utramvis plani partem constitutum trahatur: dico quod solidi vis illa attractiva, in recessu ab ejus superficie plana, decrescet in ratione potestatis, cujus latus est distantia corpusculi a plano, & Index ternario minor quam Index potestatis distantiarum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers a solid bounded by a plane on one side and otherwise infinite, made of equal attracting particles whose forces decay faster than inverse-square: shows that the total attraction perpendicular to the plane decays as a power of the distance from the plane, with exponent one less (ternary index lower by one) than the exponent of the pointwise decrement. Constructive geometric partitioning of layers (planar strips) leads to the stated result. This is the start of treatments of planar and half-space distributions.
